metaDescription: Braun MultiQuick hand blenders compared: the MQ5, MQ515, Vario 5, MQ7 and MQ9 sorted by bell design, speed control and attachment sets.
expertTake: The Braun MultiQuick 9 is the top pick if you will actually use the attachments, since its ActiveBlade shaft and three-mode control do work the cheaper sticks cannot. The MultiQuick 5 with 350W is the value pick, because it keeps the bell-shaped shaft that makes the range worth buying. Skip the 7 and 9 if all you do is puree soup, since the plain 5 series covers that for much less.
introParagraphs: One German maker has built most of its reputation on a single idea: a bell-shaped guard over the blade that cuts splatter and suction on the pan. Everything else in its hand blender family is a variation on that bell, with more speed control, a flexible shaft, or a bundle of attachments.

Choosing within one maker's range is mostly about control and extras. A 21-speed dial and a three-mode switch sound similar but feel different at the stove. This guide compares each model by what you hold, what you can attach and how quickly you will outgrow it.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 9 hand blender with 6 attachments
products.description:
The MultiQuick 9 is the flagship of the Braun range and the only one here built around ActiveBlade. The shaft is flexible and the blade moves up and down while it spins, which the listing credits with a 2.5x larger active cutting zone and 40 percent less effort. In practice that means a smoother puree from tough fibrous ingredients like celery root, and less of the pushing and tilting you do with a fixed blade.

Control comes from the iMode switch, three defined ranges of low, high and pulse, layered with the single-hand SmartSpeed trigger. That is a more deliberate interface than the dial on the 21-speed Vario 5, and it suits cooks who prefer to feel the speed through the trigger rather than read a number. Six attachments ship in the box, which makes it the most complete kit in this roundup short of the eight-attachment MQ9187XL variant.

Expect a bulkier storage footprint than a plain stick, because the attachments need a drawer. Rinse the blending shaft right away under warm water and wash the chopper and whisk by hand or in the dishwasher where the manual allows. Check that the flexible shaft section sits clean and dry in the coupling before you store it, since trapped soup is the usual reason a flexible shaft smells over time.
products.bestFor: Cooks who will use the attachments and want the smoothest puree from tough ingredients.
pros: ActiveBlade flexible shaft widens the cutting zone
iMode gives low, high and pulse ranges
Six attachments cover chopping and whisking
Single-hand SmartSpeed trigger
cons: More expensive than the 5 series for plain soup

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 7 3-in-1 hand blender and food processor
products.description:
The MultiQuick 7 trades the iMode switch of the 9 for something simpler: Easy SmartSpeed, a trigger with no predefined speed settings that ramps with finger pressure. It keeps the ActiveBlade flexible shaft, so the blade moves up and down while spinning, and it bundles a food processor attachment alongside the blending shaft. That is the angle that sets it apart, because it replaces a small countertop chopper for many kitchens.

The lack of fixed speeds will appeal to people who dislike counting, but it asks for a little control at the start of a blend. Squeeze lightly until the vortex forms, then ramp up. Compared with the Vario 5, which offers 21 numbered speeds, the 7 feels more intuitive and less precise when you want to repeat the same texture.

Because there is a food processor bowl in the box, plan for storage and for washing a gasketed lid. Wash the bowl and blades by hand after chopping onions or garlic, since odors can linger in plastic. The blending shaft should be rinsed before soup dries on the bell, and the motor body wiped with a damp cloth only.
products.bestFor: People who want one motor to replace a hand blender and a small chopper.
pros: Food processor attachment replaces a countertop chopper
Trigger ramps speed without fixed steps
ActiveBlade shaft lifts and lowers the blade
Compact bundle for a small kitchen
cons: No numbered speeds for repeatable textures
Plastic bowl absorbs strong odors over time

products.name: Braun MultiQuick Vario 5 500W 21-speed with TurboBoost
products.description:
The Vario 5 is the model for cooks who want to dial the speed precisely. Twenty-one steps plus a TurboBoost button let you start a delicate sauce slowly, then ramp into a smooth puree without swapping tools. The 500 watt motor is rated higher than the 350 watt MultiQuick 5 and the 400 watt MQ5027 in this lineup, which shows up in how little it bogs under a dense puree.

PowerBell VPlus is the bell shaped shaft of the family. The listing credits it with finer results, and the SplashControl geometry places the blades deep inside the bell to cut splatter. An EasyClick coupling lets you move between the blending shaft and the whisk with one push.

That precision comes with a bigger number of settings to learn. Most cooks end up using only three or four, so the extra dial range is wasted if you are happy with low, medium and turbo. Rinse the bell promptly, and take care that the EasyClick joint is dry before you store the unit, since a damp coupling can corrode over time.
products.bestFor: Cooks who vary texture constantly and want fine control from a single dial.
pros: 21 speeds plus TurboBoost for fine control
500W is the strongest motor in the 5 series here
Bell shape reduces splatter on the pan
EasyClick swaps attachments fast
cons: Many speed steps are rarely used
No chopper bowl in this configuration

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 MQ515 500W dual speed, beaker and whisk
products.description:
The MQ515 gives you a 500 watt motor in a plain two-speed body, which is the sweet spot for most home kitchens. It uses PowerBell VPlus with a milling blade, and the listing promises seven times finer results than a conventional stick. EasyClick Plus switches between blending and whisking in a single push, and the beaker and whisk are in the box.

The tradeoff versus the Vario 5 is control, not power. You get two defined speeds rather than twenty-one, so repeating a specific texture depends on how long you hold the trigger. For soups, smoothies and dressings that is enough, and the lack of a dial means less to break.

Because the motor is rated the same 500 watts as the Vario 5, you give up fine speed control and gain simplicity. Wash the beaker and whisk in the dishwasher if the manual allows, and rinse the bell by hand. If you only keep one stick for everyday soup and sauce work, this is a sensible landing point in the range.
products.bestFor: Everyday soups, sauces and shakes where two speeds are plenty.
pros: 500W motor at the 5-series level
Beaker and whisk come in the box
EasyClick Plus swaps heads in one push
Two speeds are simple to operate
cons: Only two speeds for texture matching

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 Vario MQ5027 400W with masher and chopper
products.description:
The MQ5027 is the accessory-heavy member of the 5 series, built around a 400 watt motor, a stainless steel blending shaft and a kit that includes a 1.5 cup chopper, a masher, a whisk and a beaker. The masher is the standout, because it lets you mash cooked potatoes or beans without shearing starch the way the blade would.

It uses the original PowerBell design with ultra-hard stainless blades and the bell shaped shaft that reduces suction. At 400 watts it sits between the 350 watt MultiQuick 5 and the 500 watt Vario 5, which is plenty for soups and sauces but a step down for dense purees.

The extras are the reason to buy it. A chopper handles onions and herbs, and the masher makes this a better fit for family cooking than a bare stick. Wash the accessories separately after use and keep the masher plate free of dried potato, which can harden quickly. Store the kit together, since the small chopper blade is easy to lose in a drawer.
products.bestFor: Families who want a masher and chopper along with the stick.
pros: Masher attachment avoids gluey potatoes
Chopper handles onions and herbs
400W motor suits everyday cooking
Beaker and whisk included
cons: 400W trails the 500W models on thick purees
Many small parts to store and wash

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 350W dual speed with beaker and whisk
products.description:
This is the cheapest Braun in the lineup and the one that proves the bell design, not the wattage, is the point of the family. A 350 watt motor drives ultra-hard stainless blades inside a patented PowerBell, and the listing highlights SplashControl, where the blades sit deep inside the floral bell shape to nearly eliminate splatter. The beaker and whisk are included.

Against the MQ515 it has 150 fewer watts and the older bell, so it slows under thick mixtures sooner. Against the MQ5027 it offers fewer accessories. For soup made from soft cooked vegetables, smoothies and dressings it is more than adequate, and its two speeds keep the interface simple.

Splatter control is the practical benefit. Push the bell flat to the pan floor before you start, then tilt slightly to let food rise into the blade. Rinse the bell under running water right away, because dried soup in the narrow slots is slow to clean. Lightweight and plain, it is a good first stick.
products.bestFor: Budget-minded cooks who want the bell design without the extras.
pros: Cheapest model in the range here
PowerBell cuts splatter on the pan
Beaker and whisk included
Two simple speeds

buyingCriteria.explanation: The bell shaped shaft is the reason to buy this maker's sticks. SplashControl places the blades deep in the bell, so a MultiQuick 5 at 350W splatters less than many wider budget sticks. Always seat the bell flat on the pan floor before switching on, which is the mistake most buyers make.

The Vario 5 gives 21 numbered speeds plus TurboBoost, the MultiQuick 9 uses three iMode ranges, and the MultiQuick 7 uses a trigger with no fixed steps. Pick the style that matches how you cook. If you repeat the same texture, numbers help; if you cook by feel, a trigger is easier.

The family spans 350W on the base MultiQuick 5, 400W on the MQ5027 and 500W on the MQ515 and Vario 5. Choose 500W if you puree dense beans or frozen fruit regularly. For soups made from soft cooked vegetables, 350W to 400W is enough.

ActiveBlade on the 7 and 9 moves the blade up and down while it spins, widening the cutting zone. It pays off with fibrous vegetables and nuts where a fixed blade pushes food away. If you mostly make smooth soup, the cheaper PowerBell sticks do the same work.

The MQ5027 brings a masher and 1.5 cup chopper, while the MultiQuick 9 adds six attachments. The 350W MultiQuick 5 gives only a beaker and whisk. Count what you will genuinely use, since every extra piece is another thing to wash and store.

EasyClick and EasyClick Plus let you pop heads on and off, but a wet coupling can corrode. Rinse the bell, dry the connection and store the unit upright. The simpler 5 series has fewer joints to maintain than the 9.

specDecoder.meaning: A bell shaped shaft covers the blade, trapping food above it and cutting suction against the pan floor. It also reduces splatter.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MultiQuick 5 at 350W uses the original PowerBell, while the MQ515 uses the VPlus version.

specDecoder.meaning: A flexible shaft section lets the blade travel up and down as it spins. This widens the cutting zone and lowers effort on tough ingredients.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the MultiQuick 7 and 9 list this feature.

specDecoder.meaning: Many steps let you start slow and ramp up gradually. Most cooks use only a handful.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Vario 5 offers 21 speeds plus TurboBoost, while the MQ515 offers two.

specDecoder.meaning: A three-range control: low, high and pulse. It is simpler than a dial but more structured than a trigger.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MultiQuick 9 uses iMode with the SmartSpeed trigger.

specDecoder.meaning: Input power under load, which sets how well the motor holds speed in thick food. Peak ratings overstate sustained output.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bell and shaft design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared each model's bell type, from original PowerBell to PowerBell VPlus and ActiveBlade. We looked at how each one is described to manage splatter and suction. The spec sheet claim of finer results on the VPlus models was treated as a manufacturer claim, not a measurement.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control interface
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 21 speeds, two speeds, iMode and trigger-only control. The question was how repeatable a texture is. A numbered dial wins for repeatable sauces, a trigger wins for improvised work.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor power spread
howWeEvaluated.description: We lined up 350W, 400W and 500W models against dense purees and frozen fruit use. The Vario 5 and MQ515 at 500W lead, the MQ5027 at 400W sits mid, and the base MultiQuick 5 at 350W trails. Owner feedback patterns informed where each begins to labour.

howWeEvaluated.title: Attachments and cleanup
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted accessories, from the six on the MultiQuick 9 to the chopper and masher on the MQ5027. We also considered how many parts you wash after each use. A smaller kit often means the stick gets used more often.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value inside the range
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the six models by relative price tier, with the 350W MultiQuick 5 cheapest and the MultiQuick 9 priciest. Each step up should buy something real: power, control or attachments.

cards.label: Numbered dial
cards.text: The Vario 5 with 21 speeds lets you repeat the same sauce texture every time and start slow to avoid splatter. It suits methodical cooks and recipe followers.

cards.label: Trigger control
cards.text: The MultiQuick 7 uses Easy SmartSpeed with no predefined speeds, and the MultiQuick 9 pairs a trigger with iMode ranges. These suit cooks who prefer feel and quick adjustment.

howToChoose.note: Pick the Vario 5 if you want repeatable settings, the 7 or 9 if you cook by feel.

rows: Masher avoids gluey starch from the blade

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A short list of parts, a dishwasher-safe beaker and a storage footprint that fits a drawer. A big attachment set becomes clutter fast.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Braun MultiQuick 5 MQ515 keeps the kit to a stick, beaker and whisk, while still delivering 500W of motor.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook fibrous vegetables, nuts or large batches, where the MultiQuick 9 and its ActiveBlade shaft earn their cost, or want the Vario 5's fine control.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You mostly blend soft vegetable soup and shakes. The MultiQuick 5 at 350W gives you the bell and the build.

maintenance.why: Dried soup in the narrow bell slots is slow to clean. Hold the bell under warm running water while the stick runs briefly.
A damp coupling traps moisture and can corrode. Wipe the joint and let it air out before reassembly.
Chopper and masher parts hold odors and dried food. Check the manual for dishwasher guidance on each piece.
Use a damp cloth only and never submerge the body. Grease from sauces builds up on the grip over time.
Do not wrap the cord tightly. Check near the handle for nicks that can become a shock risk.

faq.q: Which Braun hand blender is best for most people?
faq.a: The MultiQuick 5 MQ515 at 500W suits most kitchens, with two speeds and the bell design. Step up to the Vario 5 for 21 speeds or the MultiQuick 9 for ActiveBlade.

faq.q: Is the MultiQuick 9 worth the premium over the 5 series?
faq.a: Only if you use the flexible shaft and attachments. For soft soup and shakes the 5 series does the same work. For fibrous vegetables and nuts the ActiveBlade design reduces effort.
On dense purees and frozen fruit, yes. The 350W MultiQuick 5 slows sooner, while 500W models hold speed. For soft cooked vegetables the difference is small.

faq.q: What is the benefit of a bell shaped shaft?
faq.a: It traps food above the blade and reduces suction against the pan floor, which cuts splatter. The SplashControl geometry places the blades deep inside the bell.

faq.q: Can I mash potatoes with a Braun stick?
faq.a: Use the masher attachment in the MQ5027 kit. The blade shears starch cells and releases free starch, which makes potatoes gluey.
Many are, but check the manual for each part. Wash the blending shaft by hand and keep the motor body dry.
